deck: READING SUPER BOWL RESALE FLOORS, 48-TO-72-HOUR DIPS, ONE-WEEK COLLAPSES AND GAME-DAY DUMPS
SOURCING PLAYER, COACH AND TEAM ALLOTMENTS, THEN VERIFYING, LISTING AND FLIPPING SEATS ON DIGITAL RAILS
site_ui.lead: Broker-level testimony on how Super Bowl and marquee-event seats are allocated, sourced, priced, verified and flipped, from $950 face value to $40,000-plus seats near the 50-yard line.
site_ui.summary: All 12 chapters synthesize 192 verbatim YouTube practitioner testimonies, and every quote carries timestamped inline attribution to its channel and video. Together they map the market from StubHub's 25% average commission and the NFL's 17.5-percent-per-team allocation through VIP hospitality, seat licenses, transfers, resale law and the reseller's flipping playbook.

flow: Watch prices early, let the conference-championship spike burn off, and read buyer geography, since one traveling fan base kept StubHub sales 30 to 40% ahead of the prior year.
Fill the board from players, coaches, agents and team front-door deals, which supplied about 80 percent of one broker's listings, with roster players 35 through 53 the most likely to resell.
Stay on digital rails through verified marketplaces such as NFL Ticket Exchange, reject physical tickets for a mobile-only game, and kill any listing $1,000 to $2,000 under the going market.
List the same seats on multiple sites at once, sell direct to fans to dodge secondary-site fees, and bundle a perk such as a tailgate bash to move inventory in a soft year.
Set price alerts under the current floor and target the 48-to-72-hour window before kickoff, staying out of the final rush when desperation pushes prices back up.
Gauge leftover game-day supply before betting on a collapse, and never carry unsold inventory into a soft-matchup week without an exit plan, as game-day sellers cut hardest.
